imp.generic: She was not having a good time at the party, though she pretended otherwise.
imp.author: She wore the smile she reserved for parties, funerals, and other occasions when there was nothing to be done about it.

imp.generic: He said he loved her, but she was not sure she believed him.
imp.author: He said he loved her with the conviction of a man who had just thought of it, and would, she suspected, unconvince himself by Thursday.

imp.generic: The relationship had not ended well, and she still thought about it sometimes.
imp.author: She thought of him occasionally, the way one thinks of a bad tooth after the pulling — not with longing, exactly, but with a dull and accurate memory of the nerve.

imp.generic: Spring had arrived, and everything outside looked fresh and new.
imp.author: Spring came on schedule, bright and unreasonable, full of itself as only springs can be, and she pulled the curtain against it like a woman declining an argument she knows she cannot win.

imp.generic: She had many acquaintances but sometimes felt profoundly alone.
imp.author: She knew a great many people, which is not the same thing as knowing anyone, and is in certain lights considerably lonelier.

imp.generic: It was, in the end, not a very good poem, though she had tried hard to write one.
imp.author: She had given it her best, which is the saddest thing you can say about a poem, or indeed about anything.

imp.generic: She poured herself a drink and sat down to think about what had happened.
imp.author: She poured herself a drink, because the evening had earned it, and sat down with it in the chair where she did her best and most useless thinking.

imp.generic: Their friendship had lasted many years and had grown complicated over time.
imp.author: They had been friends for so long that they had long since run out of illusions about each other and were now operating, with great warmth, entirely on grievance.

imp.generic: She decided it was better not to say anything and simply went home.
imp.author: She said nothing, which was the cleverest thing she had said all evening, and went home and gave herself full credit for it.

imp.generic: Men, she had observed, tended to mistake silence for agreement.
imp.author: She had noticed, over the years, that men heard silence as consent, which explained a great deal about the history of the world and all of her marriages.
